metadata.title: Standing Up | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master the Standing Up position in BJJ. Complete guide covering technical standup mechanics, guard recovery, and defensive positioning. Essential fundamental skill.

overview: Standing Up (also known as Technical Standup) is a fundamental defensive position and skill in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu that allows a grounded practitioner to safely return to their feet while maintaining defensive frames and preventing takedowns. This position represents a critical transition state between ground and standing combat, serving as both an escape mechanism from inferior positions and a method of disengagement when desired. The technical standup is essential for maintaining distance management, creating space, and resetting the engagement to a more favorable position. It is particularly crucial in self-defense scenarios, MMA contexts, and competitive situations where standing offers strategic advantages. The position requires precise weight distribution, balance, timing, and spatial awareness to execute safely without compromising defensive integrity. Mastery of the standing up sequence provides practitioners with autonomy over engagement range and the ability to dictate whether the match remains on the ground or returns to standing combat.
state_invariants: Base hand posted behind body with palm flat on mat, fingers pointed away from hips, supporting approximately 40% of total body weight while maintaining straight arm structure to prevent collapse
Near leg (same side as posted hand) bent with foot flat on ground, knee pointed upward, positioned close to hips to create compact base and enable explosive drive
Far leg extended forward with heel on ground, acting as defensive barrier and distance management tool, preventing opponent from closing distance or driving forward
Hips elevated off mat with weight distributed between base hand, near foot, and far heel, creating triangular base that allows for quick pivoting and movement adjustments
Torso angled at approximately 45 degrees to mat, chest facing toward opponent with head up and eyes maintaining visual contact, ready to track opponent movement and respond to attacks
prerequisites: Opponent in standing position or attempting to engage from top position
Sufficient space created through shrimping, framing, or distance management to begin standup sequence
No immediate submission threats or controlling grips that would prevent arm posting
Practitioner on their back or side with ability to rotate hips and post supporting hand
Clear understanding of weight distribution and base mechanics
Awareness of opponent's position and distance relative to legs
key_principles: Maintain strong base hand posting with locked elbow and weight distributed through palm to prevent collapse or sweep
Keep near leg (same side as base hand) bent and loaded for explosive drive when transitioning to full standing position
Use far leg as active defensive barrier, maintaining distance through heel placement and leg extension
Elevate hips immediately to create distance from mat and establish mobile base structure
Keep head up with eyes on opponent at all times to track movement and maintain spatial awareness
Never turn back toward opponent during standup sequence - maintain chest facing toward threat
Time the transition to feet with opponent's movement, standing explosively when opponent commits to forward pressure

common_errors.error: Posting base hand too close to hips, creating weak base structure
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient leverage to elevate hips properly, making sweep or collapse more likely, and reducing ability to drive to standing position
common_errors.correction: Post base hand approximately 12-18 inches behind hips with arm fully extended and locked, creating strong triangular base structure

common_errors.error: Turning head or chest away from opponent during standup sequence
common_errors.consequence: Loss of visual contact with opponent, exposure of back, and vulnerability to attacks from blind spots
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant visual contact with opponent, keep chest facing toward threat throughout entire sequence, rotate body around base hand rather than turning away

common_errors.error: Attempting to stand with both legs simultaneously without proper base
common_errors.consequence: Loss of balance, exposure to takedowns, and inability to defend or create distance
common_errors.correction: Use proper technical standup sequence: post hand, elevate hips, load near leg, drive to standing while maintaining far leg as defensive barrier

common_errors.error: Keeping hips too low to mat during standup position
common_errors.consequence: Reduced mobility, slower reaction time to opponent's movement, and easier for opponent to close distance or attack
common_errors.correction: Immediately elevate hips high off mat upon posting hand, maintaining tension in base hand and near leg to create active defensive posture

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to control or trap extended leg without response
common_errors.consequence: Loss of distance management, exposure to leg attacks or passes, inability to complete standup sequence
common_errors.correction: Actively pump and reposition extended leg, retract if gripped, and transition to alternative guard recovery rather than fighting for compromised standup

common_errors.error: Standing up without timing or awareness of opponent's position
common_errors.consequence: Vulnerability to takedowns during transition, poor positioning when reaching standing, and wasted energy on ill-timed attempts
common_errors.correction: Time standup with opponent's movement, create distance first through framing and leg extensions, then commit to standing explosively when window opens

common_errors.error: Bending base arm or allowing elbow to collapse under pressure
common_errors.consequence: Immediate loss of base structure, fall back to mat, and return to inferior bottom position with opponent advancing
common_errors.correction: Lock base arm completely straight with scapula depressed and stable, redirect pressure through bone structure rather than muscular tension

training_drills.name: Technical Standup Repetitions
training_drills.description: Practice technical standup sequence from both sides (left and right hand posts) with focus on proper base positioning, hip elevation, and smooth transition to standing position. Start slowly emphasizing correct mechanics, then gradually increase speed while maintaining quality of movement.

training_drills.name: Standup Against Pressure
training_drills.description: Partner applies moderate forward pressure while bottom practitioner executes technical standup, working on timing the transition and maintaining base integrity under pressure. Partner gradually increases pressure level as bottom player improves competency.

training_drills.name: Standup to Guard Recovery Flow
training_drills.description: Flow drill alternating between technical standup attempts and guard recovery when partner prevents standup. Develops decision-making ability and smooth transitions between standing and re-guarding options based on opponent's reactions.

training_drills.name: Standup from Side Control Escape
training_drills.description: Start in side control bottom, escape to create space, then immediately transition to technical standup position. Partner provides realistic resistance and attempts to prevent standup while allowing practitioner to work mechanics.

training_drills.name: Standup to Takedown Defense
training_drills.description: Bottom practitioner stands up while partner immediately attempts single leg or double leg takedown. Focuses on maintaining defensive posture and balance immediately after achieving standing position.

optimal_submission_paths.name: Single leg entry to leg lock
optimal_submission_paths.path: Standing up → Technical Stand Up to Single Leg → Single Leg X Guard → Inside Heel Hook

optimal_submission_paths.name: Guard recovery to back attack
optimal_submission_paths.path: Standing up → Guard Replacement → Butterfly Guard → Arm Drag to Back → Back Control → Rear Naked Choke

optimal_submission_paths.name: Standup to guillotine opportunity
optimal_submission_paths.path: Standing up → Standing Position → Opponent shoots takedown → Guillotine Setup → Guillotine Choke

expert_insights.danaher: The technical standup represents one of the most fundamental yet frequently neglected skills in Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu. From a biomechanical perspective, the position creates a stable triangular base through the strategic placement of three contact points: the base hand, the near foot, and the far heel. This configuration maximizes stability while maintaining mobility, allowing the practitioner to pivot, adjust distance, and transition to standing with minimal vulnerability. The critical element is the immediate elevation of the hips upon posting the base hand - this single action creates distance from the mat and establishes a defensive structure that makes it exceedingly difficult for the opponent to close distance or establish control. The extended far leg functions as an active barrier, using heel placement and leg extension to manage distance precisely. When executed with proper technical precision, the standup position provides complete autonomy over engagement range, allowing the practitioner to dictate whether the match continues on the ground or returns to standing combat. This positional control is invaluable in self-defense contexts and represents a fundamental skill that should be drilled with the same dedication as any guard passing or submission technique.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, the technical standup is your insurance policy against being held down by opponents who want to stall or control without advancing position. I use the standup constantly when I want to reset the engagement or force my opponent to actually engage rather than hold position. The key is being explosive and decisive with the movement - don't telegraph the standup, just execute it quickly and confidently when the window opens. I particularly like using the standup position as a bait to draw opponents into single leg attempts, which I can then counter with entries into leg entanglement systems or guillotine attacks. In no-gi especially, the standup becomes even more important because without the gi grips, it's harder for opponents to prevent you from disengaging when you decide to stand. The standup also creates excellent opportunities for re-guard entries into my preferred guard systems like butterfly or seated guard, giving me control over which guard position I'm working from rather than being forced into whatever position my opponent wants. Master the standup and you'll never feel trapped on your back - you always have the option to reset and re-engage on your terms.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: The technical standup is absolutely essential in the 10th Planet system because it gives you the freedom to choose your battles and control the pace of engagement. What's really interesting about the standup position is how it integrates with our lockdown and rubber guard systems - when opponents try to prevent the standup by grabbing the extended leg, that's actually an excellent entry into leg lock positions or deep half guard variations. I teach my students to use the standup not just as an escape mechanism but as an active offensive tool for creating reactions and entries. The standup also becomes crucial in the transition game between standing and ground fighting, especially in MMA contexts where you need to be able to move fluidly between ranges. One variation I really like is using the standup position to create angles for back attacks - as the opponent tries to prevent you from standing, you can pivot and spin to their back while they're committed to controlling your legs. The standup also sets up some excellent guillotine opportunities when opponents shoot takedowns as you're rising to your feet. Don't just think of standup as defensive - it's an active position with offensive potential if you're creative with it.
